body:
How Engineers Solve Problems: 1. Criteria are what a good design must do; constraints are the limits you must work within. Criteria: keep milk cold for at least four hours, or fit in a backpack. Constraints: no more than $5 per design, only materials from the classroom bin, or two class periods to build. 2. A first model of a design; engineers build one to test whether the idea works and to find what to improve. 3. So they would know which change made the difference; if they changed two things, they could not tell which one helped. 4. Sequence of steps: first, next, then, with each step of the design process in order; or problem and solution: warm milk is the problem and the improved box is the solution. Either is correct with evidence. 5. The failed test showed them what was wrong (heat getting in through the open top), so they knew what to change. 6. Example criteria: holds a full backpack without breaking; lets a student hang and remove a backpack easily. Example constraints: no holes in the wall, a set cost or set materials, a set size or build time.
Keep It Cold: Design an Ice Keeper: A fair test uses ice cubes of the same size, the same place and the same 60 minutes, with an unprotected cube for comparison. Data are in grams, with ice melted = mass at start − mass after 60 minutes. Typical results: insulated designs (foam, felt, bubble wrap, a lid) let much less ice melt than the unprotected cube. A strong improvement changes one thing (for example, adding a lid or a second layer) and explains that it slows heat from getting in.
Design Check: Which Cooler Should We Buy?: The best choice is Cooler A, the only one that meets every criterion and constraint: 6 hours (at least 5), $35 (no more than $40), and 1.8 kg (2 kg or less). Cooler B kept the milk cold the longest (9 hours) but costs $55, over the $40 limit, and its mass is 2,500 g = 2.5 kg, more than 2 kg. Cooler C is cheap ($20) and light (900 g = 0.9 kg) but kept the milk cold for only 3 hours, less than 5, and its zipper broke. Reasonable improvements for Cooler A: thicker insulation or a better-sealing lid, tested one change at a time.
Scoring tip: a student who chooses B or C can still earn Proficient on evidence if the data are used correctly, but scores Beginning or Developing on criteria for not checking a constraint the choice breaks.
